content.text: {"primary_meaning":"Barley has no universally settled Christian symbolic meaning. Where a broad symbolism is assigned, it most often represents humble or inexpensive sustenance through which God provides—especially provision for ordinary or poor people.","primary_basis":["Ruth 1:22; 2:17–23; 3:15–17 — the barley harvest supplies Ruth and Naomi within a narrative of providence and redemption.","2 Kings 4:42–44 — barley loaves become the means of miraculous provision for a hundred men.","John 6:9–13 — Jesus multiplies a boy’s five barley loaves to feed the multitude.","Revelation 6:5–6 — barley is depicted as less costly than wheat during scarcity, supporting its association with basic or poorer food.","Judges 7:13–15 — the barley loaf in the Midianite’s dream represents Gideon’s seemingly humble or unimpressive force overcoming Midian."] ,"alternatives":[{"meaning":"Firstfruits, resurrection, or new life. Because barley was an early-ripening grain associated with the Passover season, some typological teaching connects it with Christ’s resurrection and the firstfruits of a coming harvest.","basis":["Leviticus 23:10–14 — the first sheaf is offered during the Passover-season festival, although the text does not explicitly call it barley.","Ruth 1:22 — Ruth arrives at the beginning of barley harvest, sometimes interpreted typologically as the start of new life.","John 6:4,9 — Passover and barley loaves occur together in the feeding narrative.","1 Corinthians 15:20–23 — Christ is called the firstfruits, though barley is not mentioned."],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"Humility, weakness, poverty, or low social status, considered apart from the broader theme of divine provision.","basis":["Judges 7:13–15 — a barley loaf signifies Gideon and his army in the dream.","John 6:9 — the miracle begins with inexpensive barley loaves supplied by a boy.","Revelation 6:6 — barley is priced below wheat."],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Harvest blessing, covenant faithfulness, and redemption, especially in interpretations of Ruth.","basis":["Ruth 1:22; 2:20–23; 3:15–17; 4:13–17 — the barley harvest forms the setting for provision, kinship redemption, and restoration."],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Scarcity, hardship, judgment, or subsistence conditions.","basis":["Ezekiel 4:9–13 — barley appears in siege rations and enacted judgment.","Revelation 6:5–6 — rationed grain prices portray famine or severe economic distress.","Exodus 9:31 — barley is destroyed in the plague of hail."],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"A fixed sacramental or prophetic code in which barley consistently denotes a particular class of believers, historical era, or eschatological group.","basis":["Such readings generally depend on extended typological systems rather than an explicit biblical definition of barley."],"prominence":"rare"}],"has_settled_consensus":false,"confidence":"high","notes":"Biblical passages use barley literally in several distinct settings, and Christian interpretation draws different contextual themes from them. The strongest recurring association is humble, ordinary provision, but it does not amount to a universally recognized symbolic definition."}
